questions.question: Which modulation technique provides better noise immunity? a). Amplitude b). FM c). PM d). ASK
questions.solution_html:
• (c)PM
  • 3D Radiation Pattern
  • • Shows radiation in all directions (three-dimensional view)
  • • Looks like a sphere, doughnut, or complex shape depending on antenna type
  • • Example: A simple dipole has a doughnut-shaped pattern
  • Low Pass Filter (LPF)
  • • Allows low frequencies to pass
  • • Attenuates high frequencies
  • • Used for noise reduction and smoothing
  • Bandwidth Efficiency vs Noise Immunity
  • • Higher-order modulation
  • o High data rate
  • o Requires high Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)
  • • Lower-order modulation
  • o Reliable communication
  • o Lower data rate

  • A carrier signal in communication electronics is a high-frequency signal used to carry
  • information (message signal) from a transmitter to a receiver.
  • Definition
  • A carrier signal is typically a sinusoidal waveform (like a sine wave) that by itself contains no
  • information, but it becomes useful when we modify it using a message signal.
  • Why we need a carrier signal
  • Low-frequency signals (like audio) cannot travel long distances efficiently. So we
  • • Combine the message signal with a high-frequency carrier
  • • This process is called modulation
  • Basic form of a carrier signal
  • (Waveform)
  • A carrier signal can be represented as
  • c(t)=Asin(2πft+ϕ)
  • Where
  • • A = Amplitude
  • • f = Frequency (high frequency)
  • • ϕ= Phase

questions.question: Design and simulate a basic RC low-pass or band-pass filter. Plot the frequency response. Identify the cut-off frequency.
questions.solution_html:

  • 2D Radiation Pattern
  • • A cross-sectional view of the 3D pattern
  • • Usually plotted in
  • o Polar form (most common)
  • o Rectangular form
  • • Easier to analyze and widely used
  • Important Terms
  • Main Lobe
  • • The region of maximum radiation
  • • Direction where antenna radiates strongest
  • Side Lobes
  • • Smaller lobes in other directions
  • • Represent undesired radiation
  • Back Lobe
  • • Radiation in the opposite direction of main lobe
  • Nulls
  • • Directions where radiation is zero or minimum
  • Beamwidth
  • Half Power Beamwidth (HPBW)
  • • Angle between points where power drops to half (−3 dB) of maximum
  • • Indicates directivity of antenna
  • Narrow beamwidth = highly directional antenna
  • Wide beamwidth = less directional
  • High Pass Filter (HPF)
  • • Allows high frequencies to pass
  • • Blocks low frequencies
  • • Used to remove DC or low-frequency noise
  • Power Requirement
  • • Higher-order schemes need more transmit power to maintain accuracy
  • • Otherwise, error rate increases

questions.question: Establish wireless communication between two nodes using NRF24L01. Transmit a simple data value. Verify successful reception.
questions.solution_html:
• (Correct Explanation of given points 5 marks)
  • The bandwidth–data rate trade-off is a key concept in modern wireless communication
  • especially when using higher-order modulation schemes.
  • Basic Idea
  • To transmit data faster (higher data rate), you generally need
  • • More bandwidth, OR
  • • More bits per symbol (using advanced modulation)
  • But increasing one often affects the other.
  • Role of Modulation
  • Lower-order modulation (e.g., BPSK, QPSK)
  • • Fewer bits per symbol
  • • Requires more bandwidth for high data rates
  • • Very robust (works well in noisy conditions)
  • Higher-order modulation (e.g., 16-QAM, 64-QAM, 256-QAM)
  • • More bits per symbol
  • • Achieves higher data rate within the same bandwidth
  • • Less robust (more sensitive to noise and interference)
  • Key Relationship
  • Data Rate=Bandwidth ×Spectral Efficiency
  • Spectral efficiency (bits/s/Hz) increases with higher-order modulation
  • • So, higher-order modulation → more data in same bandwidth
  • Trade-Off Explained
questions.source_exam: Official Practical Model Paper

questions.question: Set up RF transmitter and receiver modules (FS1000A & XY-MK). Transmit a digital signal. Observe received output.
questions.solution_html:
• (Definition 2 Mark, Proper explanation of given points 3 Marks
  • A link budget is a calculation used in communication systems to determine the received signal
  • strength at the receiver by accounting for all gains and losses in a transmission path.
  • Definition
  • A link budget is the balance sheet of power in a communication link, showing how much signal
  • power is transmitted, how much is lost, and how much finally reaches the receiver.
  • Basic idea
  • Received Power=Transmitted Power+Gains−Losses
  • Components of a link budget
  • Transmitter Power (Pt) – power sent from transmitter
  • Antenna Gains (Gt, Gr) – gain of transmitting and receiving antennas
  • Path Loss – loss due to distance (free space loss)
  • Other Losses – atmospheric loss, cable loss, fading, etc.
  • Received Power (Pr) – final power at receiver
  • Expanded formula (in dB)
  • Pr=Pt+Gt+Gr−Lp−Lother
questions.source_exam: Official Practical Model Paper

questions.question: LNA mainly improves a). Bandwidth b). Power efficiency c). Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) d). Carrier frequency
questions.solution_html:
• (Difference between dB and dBm any 5 points (5 marks), each point (1 mark))
  • dB (decibel)
  • Definition
  • dB is a relative unit used to express the ratio between two power levels.
  • Formula
  • dB=10log⁡10(P1/P2)
  • Key Points
  • • No absolute value → always compares two quantities
  • • Used for gain, loss, amplification, attenuation
  • • Can be positive or negative
  • Example
  • • Gain of amplifier = 20 dB
  • • Loss in cable = −3 dB
  • dBm (decibel-milliwatt)
  • Definition
  • dBm is an absolute unit used to measure power with reference to 1 milliwatt (mW).
  • Formula
  • dBm=10 log10(P/1 mW)
  • Examples
  • • 0 dBm = 1 mW
  • • 10 dBm = 10 mW
  • • 20 dBm = 100 mW

questions.solution_html:
• (Comparison between dB and dBm any 5 points (5 marks), each point (1 mark))
  • LC Oscillator
  • An LC oscillator uses an inductor (L) and capacitor (C) as a tank circuit to generate oscillations.
  • Features
  • Frequency determined by LC circuit f=1/2πLC
  • Examples: Hartley, Colpitts oscillators
  • Advantages
  • • Simple design
  • • Tunable (frequency can be varied by changing L or C)
  • • Suitable for RF applications
  • Disadvantages
  • • Less frequency stability
  • • Affected by temperature and component variations
  • • Lower accuracy
  • Crystal Oscillator
  • A crystal oscillator uses a quartz crystal that works on the piezoelectric effect.
  • Features
  • • Very precise natural frequency
  • • Crystal acts like a highly stable resonant circuit Advantages
  • • Excellent frequency stability
  • • Very high accuracy
  • • Low drift with temperature
  • Advantages
  • Very good frequency stability
  • High precision
  • Low power consumption
  • Disadvantages
  • • Not easily tunable
  • • Slightly more expensive
  • • Limited frequency range (fixed frequencies)

questions.question: Compare licensed and unlicensed spectrum bands. Discuss their advantages, disadvantages and applications.
questions.solution_html:
• ( Correct explanation of both spectrum 2 mark, anyone(1 mark), examples for
  • both 1 mark, Advantages and disadvantages 2 marks)
  • Licensed Spectrum Bands
  • These are frequency bands that require official permission (license) from regulatory authorities
  • (like TRAI in India).
  • Features
  • • Allocated to specific users (telecom operators, broadcasters)
  • • Exclusive use → minimal interference
  • • Requires payment (auction/fees)
  • • Highly regulated
  • Examples of Use
  • • Mobile networks (2G, 3G, 4G, 5G)
  • • TV broadcasting
  • • Satellite communication
  • Advantages
  • • Reliable communication
  • • Better quality (less noise/interference)
  • • Secure and controlled
  • Disadvantages
  • • Expensive
  • • Limited availability
  • Unlicensed Spectrum Bands
  • These bands can be used without a license, but must follow certain rules.
  • Features
  • • Open for public use
  • • Shared spectrum → more interference possible
  • • No licensing cost
  • • Limited power restrictions
  • Examples of Use
  • • Wi-Fi (2.4 GHz, 5 GHz)
  • • Bluetooth
  • • Cordless phones
  • Advantages
  • • Free to use
  • • Easy access
  • • Supports innovation (IoT devices, etc.)
  • Disadvantages
  • • Interference and congestion
  • • Less reliable
  • • Limited range/power

questions.question: Explain the bandwidth–data rate trade-off in modern wireless systems using higher order modulation schemes.
questions.solution_html:
• (Correct Explanation of given points 5 marks)
  • The bandwidth–data rate trade-off is a key concept in modern wireless communication
  • especially when using higher-order modulation schemes.
  • Basic Idea
  • To transmit data faster (higher data rate), you generally need
  • • More bandwidth, OR
  • • More bits per symbol (using advanced modulation)
  • But increasing one often affects the other.
  • Role of Modulation
  • Lower-order modulation (e.g., BPSK, QPSK)
  • • Fewer bits per symbol
  • • Requires more bandwidth for high data rates
  • • Very robust (works well in noisy conditions)
  • Higher-order modulation (e.g., 16-QAM, 64-QAM, 256-QAM)
  • • More bits per symbol
  • • Achieves higher data rate within the same bandwidth
  • • Less robust (more sensitive to noise and interference)
  • Key Relationship
  • Data Rate=Bandwidth ×Spectral Efficiency
  • Spectral efficiency (bits/s/Hz) increases with higher-order modulation
  • • So, higher-order modulation → more data in same bandwidth
  • Trade-Off Explained

questions.question: Differentiate between d B and d Bm.
questions.solution_html:
• (Difference between dB and dBm any 5 points - (5 marks) , each point - (1 mark) dB (decibel) Definition dB is a relative unit used to express the ratio between two power levels. Formula dB=10log⁡10(P1/P2) Key Points
  • • No absolute value → always compares two quantities
  • • Used for gain, loss, amplification, attenuation
  • • Can be positive or negative Example
  • • Gain of amplifier = 20 dB
  • • Loss in cable = −3 dB dBm (decibel-milliwatt) Definition dBm is an absolute unit used to measure power with reference to 1 milliwatt (mW). Formula dBm=10 log10(P/1 mW) Examples
  • • 0 dBm = 1 mW
  • • 10 dBm = 10 mW
  • • 20 dBm = 100 mW

questions.question: Compare LC oscillators and crystal oscillators.
questions.solution_html:
• (Comparison between dB and dBm any 5 points - (5 marks) , each point - (1 mark)
  • LC Oscillator
  • An LC oscillator uses an inductor (L) and capacitor (C) as a tank circuit to generate oscillations.
  • Features
  • Frequency determined by LC circuit f=1/2πLC
  • Examples: Hartley, Colpitts oscillators
  • Advantages
  • • Simple design
  • • Tunable (frequency can be varied by changing L or C)
  • • Suitable for RF applications
  • Disadvantages
  • • Less frequency stability
  • • Affected by temperature and component variations
  • • Lower accuracy
  • Crystal Oscillator
  • A crystal oscillator uses a quartz crystal that works on the piezoelectric effect.
  • Features
  • • Very precise natural frequency
  • • Crystal acts like a highly stable resonant circuit Advantages
  • • Excellent frequency stability
  • • Very high accuracy
  • • Low drift with temperature
  • Advantages
  • Very good frequency stability
  • High precision
  • Low power consumption
  • Disadvantages
  • • Not easily tunable
  • • Slightly more expensive
  • • Limited frequency range (fixed frequencies)
